> > >
> > > g =~ PRI + VCI + WMI + PSI
> > > '

You can use labels to constrain parameters.  Any parameters with the same label will have the same value.  There are several examples of fixing parameters to specific values or setting free parameters to equality across groups on the lavaan web site:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

You will only be able to test invariance of higher-order "measurement" parameters for the lower-order factors whose measurement parameters are invariant across groups.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves and lavaan users,

I have read that, in general, one cannot directly interpret the coefficients from the output of a probit regression. The way to go would be to interpret the marginal effects of the regressors, that is, how much the (conditional) probability of the outcome variable changes when you change the value of a regressor, holding all other regressors constant at some values. There are different choices to set those values apparently in the literature.
I am a bit confused now with your previous response. Could you clarify please?

I would like to apply lavaan to analyse binary outcome data and I have two additional questions:

1)      In logit and probit models, crude coefficients and adjusted coefficients for confounding effects can differ not only because of confounding but also because of a rescaling of the model. As such, logit or probit coefficients from different nested models are not measured on the same scale and are therefore not directly comparable.

Yet, it seems that it is what is done when one compares direct and indirect effects in sem interpretation. So my question is how much this statistical consideration invalidates the interpretation of direct vs. indirect relationships when some outcome variables are binary in a sem analysis.

2)      In the case of multivariable logit (or probit) regressions, Karlson and colleagues (2012 doi: 10.1177/0081175012444861  Sociological Methodology  August 2012 vol. 42 no. 1 286-313. Comparing Regression Coefficients Between Same-sample Nested Models Using Logit and Probit A New Method) develop a new method that gives unbiased comparisons of logit (or probit) coefficients of the same variable (x) across same-sample nested models successively including control variables (z).

Could such adjustments be made in lavaan?

(I noticed that the authors produced a STATA scripts and no R scripts).
many thanks in advance for your help.

Best regards,
Alban

When estimator = "ML", the objective function minimized by sem() is
based on eq 96 in the Mplus technical appendices:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/techappen.pdf

On 01/07/2015 01:11 PM, Russell Rimmer wrote:
> However then I added the regression for the variable
> 'Q4.Attended.Beltane.before'. This variable is numeric and consists
> entirely of ones or zeroes. It seemed from reading the lavaan
> documentation that adding 'ordered = Q4.Attended.Beltane.before' to the
> lavaan call was sufficient for the regression.  But, I get the error
> message show at the bottom of this post.

You are using the lavaan() function, and that is driving without a seatbelt!

What happens if you use the sem() function instead? If you must use the
lavaan() function, you should keep in mind that:

- when you add the 'ordered' argument, you are switching to
'categorical' model, and this implies meanstructure = TRUE; but by
default, all the intercepts will be fixed to zero, so you need to free
them up

- you need to provide parameter(s) for the threshold(s) of all
categorical variables (in your case: Q4.Attended.Beltane.before)

Compare this:

  library(lavaan)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9

               y ~ visual + textual + speed
'

Data <- HolzingerSwineford1939
Data$y <- c(rep(1,200), rep(0,101))

fit <- sem(HS.model, data = Data, ordered = "y", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

versus

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9

               # factor variances + covariances
               visual ~~ 1*visual
               textual ~~ 1*textual
               speed ~~ 1*speed
               visual ~~ textual + speed
               textual ~~ speed

               # residual variances indicators
               x1 ~~ x1; x2 ~~ x2; x3 ~~ x3
               x4 ~~ x4; x5 ~~ x5; x6 ~~ x6
               x7 ~~ x7; x8 ~~ x8; x9 ~~ x9

               y ~ visual + textual + speed
'

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data = Data, ordered = "y")

The latter will fail. But this should work:

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data = Data, ordered = "y", auto.th <http://auto.th> = TRUE,
int.ov.free = TRUE)

Yves.

> Dear Yves and lavaan users,

> I have read that,in general, one cannot directly interpret the

> coefficients from the output of a probit regression. The way to go would
> be to interpret the marginal effects of the regressors, that is, how
> much the (conditional) probability of the outcome variable changes when
> you change the value of a regressor, holding all other regressors

> constant at some values.There are different choices to set those values

> apparently in the literature.
> I am a bit confused now with your previous response. Could you clarify
> please?

Well, you can do this yourself manually. Choose values for the
predictors (usually, for continuous predictors, we take the mean, for
categorical predictors, we take the most common category). Compute the
probit value (simply apply the regression formula), and transform to a
probability by using pnorm(). Next, you change the value of a single
predictor (say, from 10 to 11), while keeping all others predictors at
the same value. Compute the new probit value, and transform to a
probablity again.

> two additional questions:
>

> 1)In logit and probit models, crude coefficients and adjusted

> coefficients for confounding effects can differ not only because of
> confounding but also because of a rescaling of the model. As such, logit
> or probit coefficients from different nested models are not measured on
> the same scale and are therefore not directly comparable.

So far, so good.

> indirect effects in sem interpretation.

While lavaan and sem both don’t handle count data, if you’re interested in going with the graph theoretic approach to SEM, you can use the piecewiseSEM package at https://github.com/jslefche/piecewiseSEM

In brief, it takes in a list of linear, generalized linear, mixed, or other types of models, fits them, and estimate’s Fisher’s C (see Bill Shipley’s excellent papers on this) to assess whole model fit.

You can freely incorporate glms with Poisson error for count data or otherwise.

It’s under heavy development by it’s author, and he is very eager for feedback, but so far it’s working well. I’ve included some examples in my course notes and code at http://byrneslab.net/teaching/sem/ from Day 2 and Day 4.

> - The first multi-group gained me strong invariance, this means I can
> compare the groups. But can I state that de differences in the
> regressions are significant?

You would need to test a model where you constrain the regressions to be
equal versus a model where you allow them to be free (across groups).

> - The second multi-group gave me strict invariance. Can I conclude that
> both groups are equal?

The measurement instrument behaves equal in both groups. But that does
not imply the groups are equal... (ie they can have different values on
the latent variables).

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Yes. I'm guessing you're using sem() and not lavaan().

In the first model, sem() implicitly adds covariances between all of the predictors.i.e.
x1 ~~ x2
x1 ~~ m1
etc.
So you have 4 regression paths, and 6 covariances in the model.

IN the second model, m1 and m2 are no longer exogenous, so they are not correlated automatically (that's 1 df - you should add it).

The covariance between m1 and x1 has been replaced with a regression, as has m2 and x2. But the crossovers - x1~~m2 and x2~~ x1 have not been replaced. That's your other two, making three.

Jeremy

bootstrapping.
